new_statements.quote: (g) Observations: H-toned syllables always bear stress. If there is no H tone in a word, the first syllable on the left edge is stressed (i.e., positional prominence, see Hyman 2014b: 70–73). When either an [L] or [M] tone is stressed, the stress is manifested by a slight elevation in pitch and intensity. [p. 311] ... the stress rule can be formulated thus: (261) (a) Stress the leftmost [H] tone in a prosodic word (ω). (b) If there are no [H] tones, then stress the leftmost syllable. [p. 315] ... When a word has more than one [H]-toned syllable, then the leftmost [H] tone bears main stress (End Rule Left). When an [H] tone is lacking, the stress is more subtle. It manifests itself on the leftmost syllable of the stem [p. 316]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Hrusso Aka has lexical tone (surface H, M, L) and a tone-driven, prominence-based stress system: primary stress falls on the leftmost H-toned syllable of the phonological word; if the word has no H tone, stress defaults to the leftmost (initial, stem) syllable. Stress is obligatory and culminative (one primary stress per phonological word), predictable, computed from the left edge, weight-insensitive, unbounded (not at a fixed distance from an edge), and audible as elevated pitch and intensity; stressed vowels never undergo high-vowel deletion/devoicing.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 316: additional (non-leftmost) [H]-toned syllables 'resemble secondary stress' and are called 'secondary-stressed [H] tones'; primary [H] shows anticipatory F0 slope and post-stress declination even when secondary-stressed [H] tones are present.
new_statements.exceptions: fn 168 p. 315: rule may need to refer to the 'leftmost syllable of the stem', since prefixes do not seem to host stress (fn 170: prefixes bear stress only if H-toned); fn 169: rare stressless monosyllables (e.g. unit 35 in table 63) may be clitics. Note the author's own earlier MPhil (2015: 88) analysed main stress as End Rule RIGHT (rightmost H); the 2021 DPhil replaces this with End Rule Left.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (ω), defined in §7.8.1 (p. 317) as the domain of stress and of high-vowel deletion; analysis is of continuous narrated speech (story hru_1241, 102 words, table 63), not citation forms.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Hrusso Aka (community spelling; 'Hruso'/'Hruso Aka' are exonymous spellings), the language of hrus1242, West Kameng district, Arunachal Pradesh; the stress analysis is based on a narrated text recorded at Palizi village (ELAR deposit hru_1241). The thesis (p. 15-16, §1.6.2) notes that Shafer's (1947) 'Hruso A/B dialects' were in fact two languages (Sajolang/Miji and Hrusso Aka) and that Koro Aka (koro1317) is a separate, unrelated language; Nimasow 2017 lists three minor varieties. No dialect restriction stated for the stress rule.

sources.locator: §7.8, (257g) p. 311 (PDF p. 346) and rule (261) p. 315 (PDF p. 350); criteria (262) p. 316; summary p. 316
sources.note: Ch. 7 'Tone and stress', §7.8 Stress (pp. 309-317): metrical-grid analysis of a narrated text; H-toned syllables always bear stress, the leftmost [H] in the prosodic word takes main stress (End Rule Left), and a word with no [H] stresses its leftmost (stem) syllable; stress is obligatory, culminative, predictable, demarcative from the left edge, non-moraic, audible (elevated pitch and intensity); non-leftmost [H] tones resemble secondary stress; unbounded (not edge-adjacent).
